claim: Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) and its prodrug monomethyl fumarate (MMF) are currently the most widely used agents for the treatment of multiple sclerosis (MS).
source: Monomethyl fumarate (MMF) and its prodrug dimethyl fumarate (DMF) are currently the most widely used agents for the treatment of multiple sclerosis (MS).
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Not all patients benefit from DMF treatment.
source: However, not all patients benefit from DMF.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to clinical evidence in the manuscript.

claim: Mice subjected to experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) did not benefit from DMF treatment when fed a lauric acid (LA)-rich diet.
source: In support of this hypothesis, mice subjected to experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a model of MS, did not benefit from DMF treatment when fed a lauric acid (LA)-rich diet.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 showing clinical scores and outcomes.

claim: Mice on normal chow (NC) diet showed protective DMF effects in EAE.
source: Mice on normal chow (NC) diet, in contrast, and even more so mice on high-fiber (HFb) diet showed the expected protective DMF effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mice on high-fiber (HFb) diet showed the strongest protective DMF effects in EAE.
source: Mice on normal chow (NC) diet, in contrast, and even more so mice on high-fiber (HFb) diet showed the expected protective DMF effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DMF lacked efficacy in the LA diet-fed group despite similar resorption.
source: DMF lacked efficacy in the LA diet-fed group despite similar resorption and preserved effects on plasma lipids.
evidence: This is supported by MMF plasma concentration measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The protective effect of DMF treatment on HFb diet depended on hydroxycarboxylic receptor 2 (HCAR2).
source: When mice were fed the permissive HFb diet, the protective effect of DMF treatment depended on hydroxycarboxylic receptor 2 (HCAR2), which is highly expressed in neutrophil granulocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing loss of DMF effect in Hcar2-/- mice.

claim: HCAR2 is highly expressed in neutrophil granulocytes.
source: When mice were fed the permissive HFb diet, the protective effect of DMF treatment depended on hydroxycarboxylic receptor 2 (HCAR2), which is highly expressed in neutrophil granulocytes.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing mRFP expression in neutrophils from Hcar2mRFP mice.

claim: Deletion of Hcar2 in neutrophils abrogated DMF protective effects in EAE.
source: Indeed, deletion of Hcar2 in neutrophils abrogated DMF protective effects in EAE.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 showing loss of DMF effect in Hcar2nKO mice.

claim: Diet had a profound effect on the transcriptional profile of neutrophils.
source: Diet had a profound effect on the transcriptional profile of neutrophils and modulated their response to MMF.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Diet modulated neutrophil response to MMF.
source: Diet had a profound effect on the transcriptional profile of neutrophils and modulated their response to MMF.
evidence: This is supported by functional assays in Figure 10 showing diet-dependent effects of MMF on neutrophil adhesion and NET formation.

claim: DMF required HCAR2 on neutrophils for its therapeutic action.
source: In summary, DMF required HCAR2 on neutrophils as well as permissive dietary effects for its therapeutic action.
evidence: This is supported by data from neutrophil-specific Hcar2 knockout experiments in Figure 8.

claim: DMF required permissive dietary effects for its therapeutic action.
source: In summary, DMF required HCAR2 on neutrophils as well as permissive dietary effects for its therapeutic action.
evidence: This is supported by data showing diet-dependent DMF efficacy in Figure 1.

claim: In phase-III trials of DMF treatment, 64.9% of patients showed no signs of disease activity after 2 years.
source: In phase-III trials of DMF treatment, 64.9% of patients showed no signs of disease activity after 2 years (Havrdova et al., 2017), but conversely, about one-third of patients did not completely respond to DMF.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical trial.

claim: About one-third of patients did not completely respond to DMF.
source: In phase-III trials of DMF treatment, 64.9% of patients showed no signs of disease activity after 2 years (Havrdova et al., 2017), but conversely, about one-third of patients did not completely respond to DMF.
evidence: This is inferred from the clinical trial data cited.

claim: A polymorphism in the NOX3 gene that generates reactive oxygen species predicts DMF response.
source: A polymorphism in the NOX3 gene that generates reactive oxygen species predicts DMF response (Carlström et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A rare population of memory T helper cells expressing high levels of neuroinflammatory cytokines and CXCR3 reflects DMF response in MS patients.
source: Another study found that a rare population of memory T helper cells expressing high levels of neuroinflammatory cytokines and CXCR3 reflects DMF response in MS patients (Diebold et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: MMF activates the antioxidant transcription factor NRF2 by covalently binding to the regulatory factor KEAP1.
source: MMF, the active metabolite of DMF, activates the antioxidant transcription factor NRF2 by covalently binding to the regulatory factor KEAP1 (Linker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: NRF2 inhibits the transcription of inflammatory genes.
source: Subsequently, NRF2 inhibits the transcription of inflammatory genes (Kobayashi et al., 2016), a process that may contribute to the therapeutic effects of MMF.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: MMF is an agonist of the G protein-coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A) in neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, keratinocytes, and adipocytes.
source: In addition, MMF is an agonist of the G protein-coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A) in neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, keratinocytes, and adipocytes (Tang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: HCAR2 is required for the therapeutic efficacy of DMF in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).
source: Notably, HCAR2 is required for the therapeutic efficacy of DMF in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a mouse model of MS, and in two mouse models of inflammatory skin diseases (Chen et al., 2014; Suhrkamp et al., 2022; Wannick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and data in Figure 5.

claim: DMF treatment reduced neutrophil extravasation into CNS or skin.
source: In line with Hcar2 expression in myeloid cells, DMF treatment reduced neutrophil extravasation into CNS or skin (Chen et al., 2014; Wannick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Myelopoiesis in the bone marrow is stimulated in MS patients.
source: Myelopoiesis in the bone marrow is stimulated, and circulating neutrophils show signs of activation in MS patients (Rumble et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Circulating neutrophils show signs of activation in MS patients.
source: Myelopoiesis in the bone marrow is stimulated, and circulating neutrophils show signs of activation in MS patients (Rumble et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cell-specific targeting of neutrophils improved pathology in EAE models.
source: Moreover, cell-specific targeting of neutrophils improved pathology in EAE models (Khaw et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HCAR2 was initially identified as a receptor of nicotinic acid, a lipid-lowering drug.
source: Initially, HCAR2 was identified as a receptor of nicotinic acid, a lipid-lowering drug (Tunaru et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Via HCAR2, nicotinic acid reduces serum levels of free fatty acids.
source: Via HCAR2, nicotinic acid reduces serum levels of free fatty acids (Tunaru et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DMF treatment in MS patients has similar effects on serum lipids as nicotinic acid.
source: DMF treatment in MS patients has similar effects on serum lipids as nicotinic acid (Bhargava et al., 2019), supporting the notion that DMF activates HCAR2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: An endogenous agonist of HCAR2 is the fasting metabolite β-hydroxybutyrate.
source: An endogenous agonist of HCAR2 is the fasting metabolite β-hydroxybutyrate (Offermanns, 2017; Taggart et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HCAR2 activation protects against diet-induced obesity.
source: Moreover, HCAR2 activation protects against diet-induced obesity, and the metabolic effects of HCAR2 activation depend on diet (Sato et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The metabolic effects of HCAR2 activation depend on diet.
source: Moreover, HCAR2 activation protects against diet-induced obesity, and the metabolic effects of HCAR2 activation depend on diet (Sato et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Diet intervention started 14 days before immunization in the EAE experiments.
source: To test the impact of diets on the protective effects of DMF in EAE, we fed mice with LA diet, normal chow (NC) diet, or HFb diet starting 14 days before immunization (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At the onset of neurological symptoms 8–10 days after immunization, a decrease in body weight was observed.
source: At the onset of neurological symptoms 8–10 days after immunization, a decrease in body weight was observed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Oral DMF treatment (50 mg/kg, twice per day) starting 3 days after immunization did not prevent weight loss in LA-treated mice.
source: Oral DMF treatment (50 mg/kg, twice per day) starting 3 days after immunization did not prevent weight loss in LA-treated mice, but had a moderate effect in NC-fed animals and a marked effect in HFb-fed mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMF treatment had a moderate effect on weight loss in NC-fed animals.
source: Oral DMF treatment (50 mg/kg, twice per day) starting 3 days after immunization did not prevent weight loss in LA-treated mice, but had a moderate effect in NC-fed animals and a marked effect in HFb-fed mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMF treatment had a marked effect on weight loss in HFb-fed mice.
source: Oral DMF treatment (50 mg/kg, twice per day) starting 3 days after immunization did not prevent weight loss in LA-treated mice, but had a moderate effect in NC-fed animals and a marked effect in HFb-fed mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On LA diet, DMF had no effect on the neurological deficit.
source: On LA diet, DMF had no effect, while there was a trend toward better clinical scores on NC diet and a clear improvement of the neurological deficit in terms of area under the curve (AUC), maximal score, and day of onset when mice received DMF treatment on HFb diet.
evidence: This is supported by clinical score data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: There was a trend toward better clinical scores on NC diet with DMF treatment.
source: On LA diet, DMF had no effect, while there was a trend toward better clinical scores on NC diet and a clear improvement of the neurological deficit in terms of area under the curve (AUC), maximal score, and day of onset when mice received DMF treatment on HFb diet.
evidence: This is supported by clinical score data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: DMF treatment on HFb diet resulted in a clear improvement of the neurological deficit in terms of area under the curve (AUC), maximal score, and day of onset.
source: On LA diet, DMF had no effect, while there was a trend toward better clinical scores on NC diet and a clear improvement of the neurological deficit in terms of area under the curve (AUC), maximal score, and day of onset when mice received DMF treatment on HFb diet.
evidence: This is supported by clinical score data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Diet had no significant effect on MMF plasma concentrations.
source: Importantly, diet had no significant effect on MMF plasma concentrations (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MMF measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The lack of DMF efficacy in LA diet-fed mice was not due to reduced resorption.
source: In accordance with clinical guidelines that DMF may be taken with or without food (Dimethyl Fumarate: MedlinePlus Drug Information), this indicates that the lack of DMF efficacy in LA diet-fed mice was not due to reduced resorption.
evidence: This is inferred from the MMF plasma concentration data and clinical guidelines.

claim: Diet had a strong impact on plasma lipids.
source: As expected, diet had a strong impact on plasma lipids.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Saturated lipids preferentially increased on the LA diet while non-saturated lipids decreased.
source: Indeed, plotting the relative change of lipids on LA or HFb diet versus the number of double bonds demonstrated that saturated lipids preferentially increased on the LA diet while non-saturated lipids decreased (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mice on the HFb diet were characterized by higher levels of phospholipids containing non-saturated fatty acid residues.
source: In contrast, mice on the HFb diet were characterized by higher levels of phospholipids containing non-saturated fatty acid residues (Figure 2B, component 2).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Plasma concentrations of FAs 18:2 including linoleic acid increased in the order of LA, NC, and HFb diet, in parallel with the functional response to DMF treatment.
source: As an example of a non-saturated fatty acid, plasma concentrations of FAs 18:2 including linoleic acid, the precursor of arachidonic acid, increased in the order of LA, NC, and HFb diet, in parallel with the functional response to DMF treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Plasma concentrations of the SCFA acetic acid or propionic acid did not change in DMF-treated groups or between diets.
source: Plasma concentrations of the SCFA acetic acid or propionic acid did not change in DMF-treated groups or between diets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and butyrate concentrations were below the limit of quantification.
evidence: This is supported by SCFA measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Butyrate concentrations were below the limit of quantification.
source: Plasma concentrations of the SCFA acetic acid or propionic acid did not change in DMF-treated groups or between diets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and butyrate concentrations were below the limit of quantification.
evidence: This is a direct statement about measurement results.

claim: DMF significantly changed plasma lipids.
source: Although DMF did not improve the clinical EAE score in combination with LA diet, it had metabolic effects in mice fed this diet. DMF significantly changed plasma lipids (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Particularly in animals fed LA diet, DMF lowered triglycerides, mimicking the HCAR2-mediated effect of nicotinic acid.
source: Particularly in animals fed LA diet, DMF lowered triglycerides, mimicking the HCAR2-mediated effect of nicotinic acid (Tunaru et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data and citation to previous research.

claim: DMF increased some sphingomyelins and phosphatidylcholines.
source: In addition, DMF increased some sphingomyelins and phosphatidylcholines (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DMF effects on plasma lipids were more pronounced when mice were on LA diet than on NC or HFb diet.
source: DMF effects on plasma lipids were more pronounced when mice were on LA diet than on NC or HFb diet, as also shown by the separation based on component 3 of sPLS-DA (Figure 2B) only for LA diet groups.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The lipid-lowering effects are not responsible for the protection in EAE.
source: Even when DMF did not have marked effects on the lipid profile in mice fed an HFb diet, it protected against EAE, indicating that the lipid-lowering effects are not responsible for the protection in EAE.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DMF protected against EAE on HFb diet without marked lipid changes.

claim: LA diet did not interfere with DMF resorption.
source: In addition, this observation supports the drug monitoring data showing that LA diet did not interfere with DMF resorption (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the MMF plasma concentration data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Diet had a significant impact on small hydrophilic metabolites in plasma.
source: Diet had a significant impact on small hydrophilic metabolites in plasma as shown by sPLS-DA of the metabolomics dataset (Figure 3A, components 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Glycitein and equol levels were elevated in NC diet-fed mice, indicating that this diet is enriched in isoflavones.
source: Glycitein and equol levels were elevated in NC diet-fed mice, indicating that this diet is enriched in isoflavones (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Isoflavones and equol are protective in EAE.
source: Isoflavones and equol are protective in EAE (Jensen et al., 2021), but DMF treatment did not significantly change their plasma levels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DMF treatment did not significantly change plasma levels of glycitein and equol.
source: Isoflavones and equol are protective in EAE (Jensen et al., 2021), but DMF treatment did not significantly change their plasma levels.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Plasma levels of N-acetyltyrosine were higher in the HFb diet group than in the LA diet group.
source: Plasma levels of N-acetyltyrosine were higher in the HFb diet group than in the LA diet group, similar to the clinical response to DMF treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: N-acetyltyrosine stimulates the expression of Keap1, a molecular target of MMF.
source: It is interesting to note that N-acetyltyrosine stimulates the expression of Keap1, a molecular target of MMF (Matsumura et al., 2020), suggesting a mechanism for how HFb diet could enhance the response to DMF.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Plasma levels of S1P were decreased in animals fed the HFb diet compared to the LA diet.
source: In contrast to N-acetyltyrosine, plasma levels of S1P were decreased in animals fed the HFb diet compared to the LA diet (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: S1P levels were elevated in MS patients.
source: Lowering of S1P levels by HFb diet may have a permissive effect on the therapeutic effect of DMF, as S1P levels were elevated in MS patients, and functional inhibitors of S1P receptors, such as fingolimod, improve neurological deficits in MS (McGinley and Cohen, 2021; Zahoor et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Functional inhibitors of S1P receptors, such as fingolimod, improve neurological deficits in MS.
source: Lowering of S1P levels by HFb diet may have a permissive effect on the therapeutic effect of DMF, as S1P levels were elevated in MS patients, and functional inhibitors of S1P receptors, such as fingolimod, improve neurological deficits in MS (McGinley and Cohen, 2021; Zahoor et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: DMF treatment was associated with higher abundance of glutamyl-glutamine.
source: Metabolites mainly affected by DMF treatment (component 3, Figure 3A) included glutamyl-glutamine that was elevated by DMF treatment, possibly reflecting NRF2 activation by DMF as NRF2 is known to increase glutathione, a substrate for glutamyl-glutamine synthesis (Figure 3D; Hayes and Dinkova-Kostova, 2014; Li et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D and citations to previous research.

claim: DMF lowered uracil levels irrespective of diet.
source: Irrespective of diet, DMF lowered uracil levels (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Elevated uracil concentrations occur in MS patients.
source: The underlying mechanism remains unclear, but the effect may be significant because elevated uracil concentrations occur in MS patients (Lazzarino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: MS is associated with changes in the gut microbiota.
source: Clinical studies have shown that MS is associated with changes in the gut microbiota (Correale et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DMF treatment modulates the microbiota and partially reverses MS-related changes.
source: Interestingly, DMF treatment modulates the microbiota and partially reverses MS-related changes (Diebold et al., 2022b; Ferri et al., 2023; Katz Sand et al., 2019; Storm-Larsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HFb diet reduced α-diversity in comparison to LA and NC diets.
source: In accordance with others' observations (Cantu-Jungles and Hamaker, 2023), in our experiment, HFb diet reduced α-diversity, a measure of bacterial diversity within individual hosts, in comparison to LA and NC diets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by microbiota analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DMF did not affect α-diversity.
source: DMF did not affect α-diversity.
evidence: This is supported by microbiota analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: β-diversity analyses showed significant differences between the diets, but no effects of DMF treatment.
source: Also, β-diversity analyses, a measure of dissimilarity between groups, showed significant differences between the diets, but no effects of DMF treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by microbiota analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HFb diet increased butyrate-producing bacteria while lowering pro-inflammatory species.
source: In comparison to LA and NC diets, HFb diet increased butyrate-producing bacteria while lowering pro-inflammatory species (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by microbiota analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HFb diet was associated with a higher abundance of the butyrate producers Prevotella and Parabacteroides.
source: Compared to LA or NC diets, HFb diet was associated with a higher abundance of the butyrate producers Prevotella and Parabacteroides, which may correct altered levels of these bacteria reported in MS patients (Correale et al., 2022; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by microbiota analysis data shown in Figure 4C and citation to previous research.

claim: DMF treatment did not significantly affect the dietary effects of HFb diet on Prevotella and Parabacteroides abundance.
source: DMF treatment did not significantly affect the dietary effects of HFb diet on Prevotella and Parabacteroides abundance.
evidence: This is supported by microbiota analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DMF treatment was associated with higher abundance of Acetatifactor in HFb diet-fed mice.
source: In contrast, DMF treatment was associated with higher abundance of Acetatifactor in HFb diet-fed mice (Figure 4C), but this species was associated with severe deficits in EAE (Montgomery et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by microbiota analysis data shown in Figure 4C and citation to previous research.

claim: HCAR2 is required for DMF's beneficial effect in EAE when mice were fed an NC diet.
source: A previous study showed that HCAR2 is required for DMF's beneficial effect in EAE, when mice were fed an NC diet (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DMF treatment improved the neurological deficit and reduced the AUC of clinical scores in Hcar2+/+ mice on HFb diet.
source: While DMF treatment improved the neurological deficit and reduced the AUC of clinical scores in Hcar2+/+ mice, it was inactive in Hcar2-/- animals (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by EAE data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: DMF was inactive in Hcar2-/- animals on HFb diet.
source: While DMF treatment improved the neurological deficit and reduced the AUC of clinical scores in Hcar2+/+ mice, it was inactive in Hcar2-/- animals (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by EAE data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: HCAR2 mediates the DMF action on HFb diet.
source: These findings confirm that HCAR2 mediates the DMF action, also on HFb diet.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of DMF effect in Hcar2-/- mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: Almost all neutrophils were mRFP-positive, expressing the reporter at a high level.
source: In blood, we could not detect the reporter in lymphocytes, but almost all neutrophils were mRFP-positive, expressing the reporter at a high level (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Only part of patrolling Ly6Clow and Ly6Cint monocytes expressed mRFP at an intermediate level.
source: In contrast, only part of patrolling Ly6Clow and Ly6Cint monocytes expressed mRFP at an intermediate level, and almost all inflammatory Ly6Chi monocytes were mRFP-negative (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Almost all inflammatory Ly6Chi monocytes were mRFP-negative.
source: In contrast, only part of patrolling Ly6Clow and Ly6Cint monocytes expressed mRFP at an intermediate level, and almost all inflammatory Ly6Chi monocytes were mRFP-negative (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: HFb diet slightly increased mRFP expression in Ly6Cint monocytes.
source: The rate of mRFP-positive cells and expression per cell did not differ between LA and HFb diets or DMF and vehicle treatment, with the exception that HFb diet slightly increased mRFP expression in Ly6Cint monocytes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The highest expression of mRFP in blood cells was found in neutrophils, consistent with high levels of HCAR2 in neutrophils.
source: However, independent of diet and DMF treatment, the highest expression of mRFP in blood cells was found in neutrophils, consistent with high levels of HCAR2 in neutrophils (Tang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6 and citation to previous research.

claim: Microglia and monocyte-derived macrophages in the brain expressed mRFP.
source: In addition to neutrophils, microglia and monocyte-derived macrophages in the brain expressed mRFP, with HFb diet slightly increasing the mRFP expression in microglia (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: HFb diet slightly increased the mRFP expression in microglia.
source: In addition to neutrophils, microglia and monocyte-derived macrophages in the brain expressed mRFP, with HFb diet slightly increasing the mRFP expression in microglia (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nicotinic acid (100 µM) elevated [Ca2+]i in wild-type Hcar2+/+ neutrophils.
source: As shown before (Kostylina et al., 2008), nicotinic acid (100 µM) elevated [Ca2+]i and MMF (100 µM) had a similar effect (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7A-C and citation to previous research.

claim: MMF (100 µM) elevated [Ca2+]i in neutrophils.
source: As shown before (Kostylina et al., 2008), nicotinic acid (100 µM) elevated [Ca2+]i and MMF (100 µM) had a similar effect (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Stimulation with nicotinic acid was mediated by HCAR2 as it increased [Ca2+]i in wild-type Hcar2+/+ neutrophils but had no effect on neutrophils from Hcar2-/- mice.
source: Stimulation with nicotinic acid was mediated by HCAR2 as it increased [Ca2+]i in wild-type Hcar2+/+ neutrophils but had no effect on neutrophils from Hcar2-/- mice (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Hcar2+/+ and Hcar2Fl/Fl neutrophils reacted similarly to nicotinic acid and MMF stimulation.
source: Hcar2+/+ and Hcar2Fl/Fl neutrophils reacted similarly to nicotinic acid and MMF stimulation, both with respect to the response of individual neutrophils and the rate of responsive cells, indicating that the artificial intron does not interfere with Hcar2 expression (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: The artificial intron does not interfere with Hcar2 expression.
source: Hcar2+/+ and Hcar2Fl/Fl neutrophils reacted similarly to nicotinic acid and MMF stimulation, both with respect to the response of individual neutrophils and the rate of responsive cells, indicating that the artificial intron does not interfere with Hcar2 expression (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar responses of Hcar2+/+ and Hcar2Fl/Fl neutrophils.

claim: In the presence of the Ly6gCre gene, the response rate dropped significantly from 75–80% in Hcar2Fl/Fl neutrophils to about 35–40% in neutrophils from Hcar2nKO mice.
source: However, in the presence of the Ly6gCre gene, the response rate dropped significantly from 75–80% in Hcar2Fl/Fl neutrophils to about 35–40% in neutrophils from Hcar2nKO mice (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: In Hcar2Fl/Fl animals fed on HFb diet, DMF treatment had a significant effect on the neurological deficit.
source: In Hcar2Fl/Fl animals fed on HFb diet, DMF treatment had a significant effect on the neurological deficit. Interestingly, this effect was lost in Hcar2nKO mice (Figure 8A and B), demonstrating that HCAR2 stimulation of neutrophils is required for DMF therapeutic effects.
evidence: This is supported by EAE data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The DMF effect was lost in Hcar2nKO mice.
source: In Hcar2Fl/Fl animals fed on HFb diet, DMF treatment had a significant effect on the neurological deficit. Interestingly, this effect was lost in Hcar2nKO mice (Figure 8A and B), demonstrating that HCAR2 stimulation of neutrophils is required for DMF therapeutic effects.
evidence: This is supported by EAE data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: HCAR2 stimulation of neutrophils is required for DMF therapeutic effects.
source: In Hcar2Fl/Fl animals fed on HFb diet, DMF treatment had a significant effect on the neurological deficit. Interestingly, this effect was lost in Hcar2nKO mice (Figure 8A and B), demonstrating that HCAR2 stimulation of neutrophils is required for DMF therapeutic effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of DMF effect in neutrophil-specific Hcar2 knockout mice.

claim: The diet had profound effects on neutrophils' transcriptional profile.
source: The diet had profound effects on neutrophils' transcriptional profile (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Neutrophils expressed genes associated with 'regulation of cell activation', 'innate immune response', and 'negative regulation of immune system process' at a higher level in HFb diet than in LA diet.
source: According to gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis, neutrophils expressed genes associated with the terms 'regulation of cell activation', 'innate immune response', and 'negative regulation of immune system process' at a higher level in HFb diet than in LA diet (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and GO analysis data shown in Figure 9B.
